utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness in? Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Dixon and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Appearing with me on behalf of Mr. Delalic is my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic together with my colleague Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman and along with Cynthia McMurrey we appear on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The witness is just coming in and I wanted to ask you, your Honours, for permission to address you with only two sentences. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us get him sworn, then you can, please. We will swear him and then you can start. Kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let the witness take the oath. PROFESSOR ECONOMIDES (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Residovic, let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the cross-examination of Professor Economides, we would like to know what the following procedure will be. We know that the Prosecutor has mentioned a motion for hearing a new expert witness; as the Defence we object vehemently to that request and also we feel that the court should rule on this request and that they should be argued before the witness from Slovenia appears. We are also opposed to such a practice that we have to decide about such important things when the witness is already here. So that I hope that when we finish with the cross-examination of Professor Economides, could you tell us when we will be deciding on this request or motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You will hear from the Trial Chamber immediately the opportunity arises. Mr. Niemann, continue with your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The evidence-in-chief has been completed, your Honours. Now it is time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We will proceed in this order during cross-examination. First counsel for Mr. Mucic, second counsel for Mr. Delic, third counsel for Mr. Landzo and fourth counsel for Mr. Delalic. Cross-examined by MR. GREAVES

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May it please your Honours, Professor Economides, we are in the first week of December of this year. I think for you 1st December was an auspicious day in your career. Do you remember why that should be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: December 1st?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: December 1st, yes, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 4th December is my birthday, that is an important date, but 1st December is not something I can think of right off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can remind you. It was the day in 1956 when you had the privilege of defending your thesis before a jury of professors at the University of Strasbourg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a detail for me today, that is all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. I think the topic upon which you chose to address and address your thesis was: "La question cypriote et le droit des peuples a disposer d'eux memes".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Determination of peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we take it from that in the period of 41 years since you presented your thesis, the topic of self-determination of peoples has been one that has been uppermost in your professional career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say the total focus, but it is a question I have always been interested in. When I was young, it was a question about which I was passionate and since then, I have been studying that issue, but it is not one which was really at the very centre of my scientific concerns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still stand by all that you wrote in your thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Economides, I would like now to talk with you please about the work of the Venice Commission, of which you are a member. I think the proper name of the Commission is the European Commission for Democracy Through Law, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is, in fact, I think, an organ of the Council of Europe, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us about this, please: how do you get to be a member of the Venice Commission? How did you get appointed or invited to join it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all the government must make a statement that it wants to participate in the Venice Commission's work. Therefore the decision at the very beginning of the issue is a government one, that is the participation of the government in the Commission's work and it is the government itself which appoints its representatives. I was appointed twice because I had my second term within that Commission and I was nominated by the Greek Minister for Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with the work about which you told us on the last occasion you were here, I think it produced at its meeting in the 1996, September 1996, a declaration which was accompanied by an explanatory report, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in turn, the Council of Europe itself, as it were, the parent organisation, has produced a draft convention, the European Convention on Nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the two things are not linked, they are different. The Venice Commission prepared its draft which you have mentioned, that it was a draft declaration, which was followed by an explanation of the reasons and a basic report and then the Council of Europe, for a long time, well before the creation of the Venice Commission, was working on the issue of nationality, and it determined that there would be a convention -- an international convention for that issue, which was also a product of the work of the Council of Europe, but had nothing to do with the Venice Commission and its declaration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just so that we understand this, the Council of Europe is composed, I think, of some 40 states, but not including Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not yet; no doubt when matters have resolved themselves to everybody's satisfaction, that invitation will be given to them. But is it right that Bosnia-Herzegovina has in fact contributed to the work of the drawing up of the European Convention, at the invitation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite possible, because the Convention also had observers from several states, so it is very possible that Bosnia-Herzegovina was one of the states that participated in the drafting of the Convention, but as an observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also right that that treaty will be open for signatures by countries who are not members of the Council of Europe, but who are invited by the Committee of Ministers to sign if they want to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Convention has as its very objective the point that it must be open to all states; that is the largest number of states possible and probably there is a procedure which allows this or that state in the Council of Ministers to become part of the Commission so that there would be the largest number of accepting parties for the Convention possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us about this, please, Professor: what is the current status of the European Convention on Nationality? Has it been put out for signature by the member states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was open to the member states' signature and currently it is being signed, but it has not gone into effect according to what I know. In order for it to go into effect, there needs to be ratification and we do not have yet -- we have not yet reached that stage, but it is a convention which has been signed and open to signatures and which will become a convention which will be applied within a short time, but I cannot tell you exactly how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to the work of the International Law Commission, of which you are also a member, Professor, that Commission too has been working on the topic of nationality in the context of succession of states.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July 1997, it produced a report containing not just a series of commentaries on the topic but a set of draft articles on this very aspect of international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the draft -- it is in the form of, may we call it, a draft treaty, national in relation to succession of states.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That has not yet been decided. There is a trend in the Commission which we saw in its session this year was to set up a draft declaration, but after discussions, it was decided that was premature to take a decision as to the form, therefore it might possibly be a convention, but I believe that this will be decided much later. For the moment, there are draft articles, but we do not know whether these will be a draft declaration or a draft convention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to ask you about the procedure by which this might eventually become a treaty. I think it has received what is called a first reading, is that the correct phraseology?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There is the first reading, that is the first stage. After that, the governments will make comments about the draft, and the International Commission will receive all the governments' comments and then it will review once again all the drafts based on the comments from the States and will adopt the draft in the second reading, and once the draft has been accepted in the second reading, it is sent to the General Assembly of the United Nations, which will be the organ to decide whether the draft will become an international convention and in such a case, the General Assembly of the United Nations will set up an international convention, especially designed to change the convention into something more permanent. Therefore we need to wait some time before we reach an international convention, if it is going to be adopted at all, because there are still many people who state that the draft has to be transformed only into a draft declaration. If you want an estimate as to the time involved, I could tell you that the ILC will review the draft in the second reading in 1999, and the question will come up before the General Assembly again in the year 2000 and from that point on, we will see what the fate of the draft will be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so you have answered some of my next questions about the time scale for those set of draft articles. We are talking about well into the next century before it achieves the status of settled law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very close to the next century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just digress a little bit, please, and ask you about the 1978 Vienna Convention on Succession of States. You are familiar no doubt with that convention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that convention yet in force, or has it yet to achieve the requisite number of signatories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not in force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Economides, in relation to the work of the International Law Commission, you mentioned on the last occasion that from time to time, the International Court of Justice cites the work of the International Law Commission, even if the stage that has been reached is only the first leading. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the draft articles about which we have been talking this morning, has there been any case before the International Court of Justice in which that work has been cited, whether with approval or disapproval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as regards state succession, I do not think that the International Court of Justice has cited anything that comes from the International Law Commission. But as regards the question of international responsibility and other questions, which are still being codified before the International Court of Justice, the court has in fact cited the words of the ILC, but not as regards state succession. But I should tell you that the question of state succession now is reaching the first year where it is being studied and I do not think there have been any cases that have to go to the International Court of Justice in order to incite some sort of interest in it, that its work would be of any interest to the International Court of Justice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Economides, the task of the International Law Commission is twofold, is it not? First of all, the codification of the law that has been already developed on the plane of international law, and secondly the progressive development of law for the future; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In essence, when a set of draft articles is produced, it is a distillation of those two things; it is codifying that which has become settled practice in international law and effectively it is suggestions by learned gentlemen such as yourself as to what is considered the law ought to be for the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I turn now please to the question of nationality and what the definition of that is in the context of international law? Would you agree with me that the classic definition of the word "nationality" is that set out in the Nottebohm case of 1955?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just refresh your memory as to what the case actually says concerning that definition. Would you prefer me to do it in the French or the English version, which would assist you better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would prefer the French version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you shall have it in French: "As regards practice of states, the arbitral and judicial decisions and the decisions having to do with case law, nationality is a judicial link and at its base has a social desire to be attached to the effect of solidarity of existence, which is of interest of joint considerations, and the reciprocity of the right of duties. It is the legal expression of the fact that the individual on which it has been conferred is directly, by the law, or by an act coming from an authority, more closely linked to the population of a state conferring on it than it is to any other state, that has been conferred by a state, and gives it right to exist vis-à-vis another state, only if it can show that the individual is connected to that state which has made him its national." That is the accurate statement of the law, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the definition which is the most complete one and the most correct one having to do with nationality that I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is the definition which has been used as the basis for the work of all of the two commissions in which you have been working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an English textbook called, "Oppenheim's International Law"? Is that a textbook that you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a well respected textbook, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That textbook, I think, quotes the Nottebohm definition with approval and also uses this phrase and I wonder whether you would also agree with this: "Nationality of an individual is his quality of being a subject of a certain state."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to put this proposition to you, Professor, on the issue of nationality. Would you agree with me that it is clear law that the issue of who is and who is not a national of a particular state is a matter for the internal laws of that individual state, subject to the limitations that international law rules put upon it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree absolutely that it is internal law which designates who are the nationals of that state, therefore it is through internal law and the state jurisdictions which fall under the jurisdiction in each state that it can determine who its nationals are, but the determination must be made according to international laws which, as you have just said, they have to be conditional on agreement with the laws of international law, therefore it is state jurisdiction, but may be subjected to certain controls, having to do with agreements with international law and its rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That proposition was made as long ago as 1923 in the case of the nationality decrees issued in Tunis and Morocco and has gone through various treaties, a principle that has been reaffirmed time and time again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the state of law today, that within those limitations, it is for the individual state to determine who its nationals are. The effect of that is that it is not within the power of any outside agency to tell a state who its nationals should be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle you are right, but in the Nottebohm case, nationality which was conferred on Liechtenstein was not accepted by Guatemala. Therefore there was one state which did not accept a government decision which had conferred nationality. After the opposition, there were various discussions between Guatemala and Liechtenstein which were brought before the International Court of Justice, and the International Court of Justice said that it was not the national state that was right but the government who had opposed the recognition of the nationality of Liechtenstein. Therefore, your comment is correct, that is the state which grants nationality, but this is not unchallengeable in every case. It can even be overturned. It depends on whether internal laws, when applied to give nationality to somebody, are in accordance with international law, but I do agree with you that there is a general trend, and that is relevant, in which we see that the state grants nationality to its nationals, but there are exceptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to come back to the Nottebohm case in a little while, but I just want to deal with one other matter, and it is this, Professor. Would you agree with me that it is clearly the law that when a succession of states takes place which involves the dissolution of the predecessor state, the nature of the predecessor state ceases to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that cannot be challenged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the case involving the former Yugoslavia which was once known as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, when that dissolved, at that moment the nationality of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia also disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when the dissolution had occurred, the nationality of the former Yugoslavia necessarily would disappear, but I would say that when the dissolution became operative, this is a very specific issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you to tell us when that date was, I think that is a matter for others to establish. You told us on the last occasion about the means by which it is accepted internationally that people can acquire nationality, and you mentioned three means of acquisition. Can I just refresh your memory as to what you told us? They are the jus soli, and would it be right to say that that is, in broad terms, deriving your nationality from the place where you are born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, through birth on a certain territory, certain grounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the second was the jus sanguinis, which in broad terms is deriving your nationality from your family, where your parents are born and their nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third means you mentioned was naturalisation, a well known procedure by which you apply to become a national of a particular country and they accept you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The textbook Oppenheim mentioned two other means of acquisition, and I would just like you to help us and see whether you agree that they are also potential ways of acquiring nationality. One is referred to as resumption of nationality, in other words recovering a nationality that you had at some former time. Would you agree that that is a means of acquiring nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would say that that is on another level. It is an auxiliary method which is somewhat exceptional, but it does exist, but I have to make clear that the three examples that I know were not cited in order to exhaust all the cases. There are other ones as well. These were examples I was giving you, the most striking ones. There are other cases as well. In principle, I agree with Oppenheim that there were other people who give exhaustive lists of cases of when nationality was acquired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not trying to catch you out, Professor, I just want to make it absolutely clear that there are other methods and there is one more I want to mention to you. In the past, nationality has been acquired by people because their territory has been either annexed or ceded in some way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Nottebohm case which I said I would come back to, I think it is quite helpful just to look at the facts of that case so that one can extract from it the nature of the words "effective link", which I think is the phrase which is used as a means of describing somebody's nationality in the two commissions in which you have worked, is that right? That is the classic phrase, "effective link".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nottebohm I think was a German by birth, and over the years prior to the Second World War, he had established a substantial business in Guatemala. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1939 when the clouds of war in Europe were gathering, Mr. Nottebohm spotted that that might well have a serious impact on his commercial life, and so he applied for citizenship of Liechtenstein.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that stage, he had no real genuine links with Liechtenstein, other than a brother who had lived there for a while.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having acquired Liechtenstein nationality, he went and resumed his commercial life, no doubt doing his business in Germany and Guatemala, and then Guatemala declared war on Germany and so he became, as far as Guatemala was concerned, an enemy alien, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They chose thereby to ignore the fact that he had on the face of it acquired Liechtenstein nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was deported to the United States, he lost his property and it was as a result of that that action was taken by Liechtenstein to try and protect his assets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with this, that the most important aspect of the phrase "effective link" or "genuine link" is habitual residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is not the only one, but that is the one which is thought by authoritative writers on the subject to be the principal criterion of "effective link".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it would also be right to look at, for example, place of birth, place of education, career, business interests, participation in public life and affairs, voting and other family connections with a particular nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those criteria can be used, as in the Nottebohm case, to determine of which country people are nationals and indeed of which country they are not nationals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, Professor. Is there a distinction between domicile and nationality? Habitual residence may be indicative of domicile, not nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are two different things. Somebody may have the nationality of this or that state and have his domicile outside that state. He remains a national, let us say, of the United Kingdom, even though he may live in France. Most frequently, both coincide, nationality and domicile. A Greek who has Greek nationality who lives in Greece and lives with all the other millions of Greeks is there, but those are two different things, domicile and nationality. They are not the same thing. Most frequently there is a coincidence, or the two come together, but the two elements may not coincide, which was the case which I pointed out of someone who may be a national of a state but has his residence or domicile in another state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Please feel free, your Honour. Just to give an example of that, Professor, Judge Jan at the moment is plainly a citizen of the Republic of Pakistan, but at the moment he is living in The Hague and he might be thought to be domiciled in The Hague. Would that be a fair way of dealing with that aspect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, there is another element. The intention to revert back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was well aware of that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he has an international activity, he does not change domicile, according to Greek law. In other words, any Greek official working for the United Nations, for instance, is regarded as having his domicile in Athens, the capital of Greece. There is a change in domiciles if somebody settles for private reasons in another country, has professional, commercial activity in another country, which is quite legal anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I want now to turn to the three principles you enunciated concerning nationality, please, the first of which was this, and your evidence was this: "Any person involved in state succession is entitled to a nationality." That is a principle which is derived, is it not, from Article 15 of the Universal Declaration on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The date of the Universal Declaration, was that 1948?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 48.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The origin of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and correct me if I am wrong, was it very much a document that arose out of the events and consequences of the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the major extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An expression of the world community's desire that the events of that war should not happen again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the principal considerations that brought about Article 15, would it be this, that at the end of the war in 1945, particularly in Europe, there were large numbers of people who had become displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of substantial and significant changes in territorial boundaries as a result of the consequences of the war, there were large numbers of people who had become stateless.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And large numbers of people who had been expelled from territories in which they had formerly lived, for example the expulsion of ethnic Germans from Poland or Czechoslovakia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that state of affairs caused large numbers and very significantly large numbers of people who had no nationality, i.e. stateless persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that since 1945, it is statelessness which has been very much a motivating force for the succession of treaties that have been arrived at on the topic of nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is because the large numbers of stateless people caused enormous problems to the governments of Europe in the years after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think there has been a convention in 1954 relating to the status of stateless persons and then another one on the reduction of statelessness in 1961, dealing with that very topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the draft articles of the International Law Commission and the European Convention on Nationality have very much as their focus the issue of statelessness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that really covers the second principle which you enunciated to their Honours, the need for states to avoid doing or passing legislation which brings about statelessness to any person, not just large numbers of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want now to turn to the third principle which you enunciated, which is this, that a state which confers its nationality on someone or on a group of persons must respect the will of those people. You recall telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I suggest this to you, that that is not yet the settled law in international law, and I will give you a reason why that is so. It comes from Article 10 of the draft articles of the ILC draft, which says this: "States concerned shall give consideration to the will of persons concerned whenever those persons are qualified to acquire the nationality of two or more states concerned."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to suggest to you is that the present state of the law is this, that the obligation is at best upon a state to give consideration to the will of people, not to follow it completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you allow me to comment on this last observation, I should say the following. Article 6 which you have just read out is quite in keeping with your presentation, but if you were to read articles related to state succession and the ILC, in other words Article 20, "transfer from the point of view of the territory", Article 22, "state dissolution" and Article 24, "separation of a part or parts of a territory", and the following articles, you will notice that in all these articles, the ILC sees it as mandatory to have the right of option. In all cases, people have to express themselves as to their nationality and somehow as a matter -- whether they want that nationality or not. I would even say that these articles have a very wide scope. For instance, Article 20, in case of a transfer of territory, they have the right of option, not only with people having an effective link with a neighbouring country, but it applies to all people. Let us imagine in Bosnia-Herzegovina if there was no independent state but only a territory that had been given to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The question should have been put not only to the Serbs but also to the Croats to know whether they too want to be nationals of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This means that the option right seen by the International Law Commission in all types of succession goes much further and it is mandatory in all cases of succession at a very large scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, Professor. The persons who find themselves in the succeeding state, he has the option to retain the citizenship of the parent state, but supposing the parent state does not accept him, it only accepts those which are within its territory. Then what happens in that case? Citizenship is essentially, as far as municipal law is concerned, the question of relevant law, municipal law. The person finds himself in a succeeding state and he wants to opt for the parent state but the parent state will not accept him; which nationality does he enjoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relevant rights in a case of state succession, the relevant right is the right of the successor state which is being born and that state is entitled to grant its nationality to all persons having the nationality of the predecessor state and residing in the territory of the successor state. That is an absolute right which is the privilege of the successor state. On the basis of the draft articles that we have mentioned, the successor state must withdraw its nationality from the citizen that has acquired the nationality of the successor state. There is that kind of obligation, but to avoid states of statelessness, they say that the predecessor state should abstain to grant its nationality until the successor state grants its nationality to the person involved in a case of state succession. But possibly the predecessor state may decide not to withdraw its nationality, it has been noted in the past, in which case the person will enjoy dual nationality, that of the successor state granting its nationality and the nationality of the predecessor state that keeps existing. Of course, if there is dissolution there is no longer any predecessor state, but if that predecessor state keeps existing, it may decide not to withdraw the nationality from the person concerned, so that person may have dual nationality. This may occur in quite a few instances and I would say that the International Law Commission privileges dual nationality, even multiple nationality. It makes it possible for citizens to acquire several nationalities. If you read the draft articles, you will notice that a person may be entitled to obtain the nationality of one or several successor states. He can be from Slovenia and from Bosnia at the same time. It is only draft law, but these are cases that may occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not think your answer actually covered the points raised by my brother Jan. His anxiety is in the circumstance that an option is refused by the predecessor state. What happens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The option right is not granted by the predecessor state. It must be granted by the successor state. The predecessor state would only exceptionally grant that option right. For instance, in the new composition of its population there are groups of citizens that obviously do not wish to acquire that nationality, that new nationality, and want to maintain the nationality of the predecessor state, in which case the successor state must give the right of option to such people. If it fails to do so, what it does is impose by way of authority a nationality that somebody does not want, so the right of option is valid for the successor state and not for the predecessor state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: By that, you mean a citizen who is by compulsion one of the successor state cannot opt to predecessor state. Since it is only the successor state which can grant its option, it means he cannot retain his predecessor citizenship.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I possibly did not quite express myself correctly. The classical formula of the right of option is as follows. It has been noted in past history, the successor states, after a reasonable period of time, will say to a category of citizens the following: "do you want to obtain my nationality or do you wish to keep the nationality of the predecessor state?". The successor state offers this choice between two nationalities, that of the successor state and that of the predecessor state, but -- this is carried out by the successor state but individuals have then the option of choosing the predecessor state's nationality if they so wish. This is the classic procedure in the right of option. The last occasion, I mentioned the case of the Greek islands, which Greece obtained after the Second World War. One year down the track, they organised the right of option for the citizens, for the option of the Italian speaking people on those islands, and the Italian speaking individuals were granted the right to choose Italian nationality. If they decided not to choose it then they were keeping Greek nationality. That is what we did in Greece straight after the time when those islands became Greek property, as it were, but this was decided after the right of option was granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Professor, can I ask you this, please? We were talking about draft Article 10 of the International Law Commission's draft articles and I suggested to you that the wording of that draft article implies that there is no obligation to grant a right of option to the category of people mentioned in Article 10. I suggest that because that is set out in the commentary to the draft articles in precisely those terms. It says this: "The expression 'shall give consideration' implies that there is no strict obligation to grant a right of option to this category of persons concerned." Do you accept that that is the meaning that is imported by draft Article 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Similarly, the draft treaty -- sorry, the European Convention on Nationality, Article 18.2(c), with which I am sure you are familiar, has similar phraseology, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that it is plain what it says, Article 18.2 says this: "In deciding on the granting or the retention of nationality in cases of state succession, each state party concerned shall take account in particular of", and subsection (c) is: "The will of the person concerned."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the commentary to the European Convention that has been provided to us, it says this: "As regards sub-paragraph (c), the will of the person concerned has to be taken into account. This might entail, for example, giving persons a right of option, or avoiding the imposition of nationality against the wishes of a person." Again, I suggest there is no obligation contained in that article, no obligation to grant a right of option in every case, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, let me get from the Professor: these are the plain words of the draft, is it that in international law a state can compulsorily confer a citizenship on a group of persons if the new status is derived from a new situation like a war situation. Is that the meaning of that, when you forcibly take your group of people out from an existing state, international law insists that you can keep them forcibly your citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very complex issue indeed. On the basis of the principles of international law, a state may grant its nationality, for instance, in a case of state succession, following state succession and not military occupation. Indeed, in the latter case, on the basis of the law of war, a state may not, unless it violates the basic principles, it may not change the nationality of the people in the occupied territory, but when we have to do with state succession, the successor state is entitled to grant its nationality, even forcibly or by way of authority, to all of its population. This has been noticed and experienced in history, but here is the change: after some time has elapsed, that state must feel what the general feeling of the population is and open the right of option. Once the state is settled and everything is back to normal, then it must give its right of option to those who obviously do not wish to maintain the nationality that was forcibly put on them. Throughout history, we have cases of option for nationality, there are thousands of such cases, and I believe this is current international practice. So to reply to your question, I would say in a case of succession a state is entitled to grant its nationality, but not in any way, after some reasonable period of time has elapsed. It must open the right of option to such population and also to those groups that cannot acquire the nationality of the successor state. This has been noted throughout history. In the case in point in this issue we are debating, indeed we have to do with very important legal problems. Article 10 mentions the problem of option on the non-compulsory basis. The Council of Europe Convention on Nationality also has quite a flexible approach to the issue. However, the Venice Commission, which issued a declaration, sees the right of option as something compulsory. The ILC, as regards state succession, Article 20, 24, 26, which I have mentioned, sees the right of option as something compulsory, mandatory. I think we are at a given stage in the development of international law, where not everything has been crystallised. Is this an international compulsion, obligation? I believe it is, to grant the option, right. I am an internationalist, but other people may not be of that opinion. It remains that the right of option is something that is quite common in international practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am very grateful. My apprehension mainly was that if such a compulsory situation exists, and the new state has within it a substantial minority of dissident citizens, it is likely to have a snowball effect on this group of people trying to break away again, unless perhaps there is an opportunity for them to change their citizenship. If you compulsorily retain them and there is no other way of getting out of this situation, they might find a way back. That is a personal view, it has nothing to do with the current status of international law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In law, you always attempt to give ways of getting out of a problem, exit ways. In the case you have just mentioned, your Honour, you still have the option of having ex officio nationality, but there remains the obligation to open a right of option when things have settled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Professor, can I just move on please now to the question of what is the nationality of residents of a successor state. What you told their Honours on the last occasion you were here is that the rule is categorically clear, that the successor state must accord its nationality to all the nationals of the predecessor state who have their habitual residence on the successor state's territory. Can I put this to you, so that you can find the passage in the ILC draft articles. It is Article 4. It is right, is it not, that that draft article says this: "Subject to the provisions of the present draft articles, persons concerned having their habitual residence in the territory affected by the succession of states are presumed to acquire the nationality of the successor state on the date of such succession." Do you recall that draft article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This arises out of a question that the learned judge Judge Jan asked on the last occasion, about the time lag that occurs between a succession of states and the possible granting of a right of option. Do you recall the learned judge asking you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right, that the purpose of Article 4 is to address that very problem of the time lag between the date of succession of states and either the creation of legislation or the conclusion of a treaty that deals with the question of granting a right of option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 4 and Article 6 aim at directing people's attention on the need for a nationality as soon as the succession of states starts, to avoid any vacuum and have people being without any nationality. These are presumptions which, of course, are not cast in iron. They, of course, may not happen in real life, because nationality is not granted on the basis of a presumption, but by action taken by the state. These provisions say that the state has to make such legislation so as to grant nationality as soon as the succession of states starts. This has always been the case in history. The first action taken by a sovereign state who has become independent is to determine which are the nationals of the new population in this new state. So these two provisions, Article 4 and Article 6, stress that, underline that, but as principles, so that states do align themselves on such practice, which means that if a state has not granted its nationality and if a citizen will get that nationality on the basis of Article 4, to acquire nationality, you need to have an internal legislation passed by the state granting nationality to specific groups of people, inter alia to those who had the nationality of the predecessor state and reside in the territory of the new state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is a two stage process; first of all, when the succession of states takes place, a presumption comes into operation in line with Article 4, and then in due course legislation is passed by the sovereign state which sets out the basis on which people are nationals of their state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that when there is state succession, it is internal law which becomes applicable law. That is the law that counts. Everything else are guidelines as to how the law should operate. Therefore it is internal law which must immediately grant nationality as provided for in the articles that I have just cited. If there are any questions or doubts, presumption, of course, will find its place and may play a role, but if there is no internal law which grants nationality, nationality cannot be granted -- it can be conferred by this or that article being applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn now to the specifics, please, of rights of option? Would you agree with this proposition, Professor, that when we talk of a right of option, there are two possible things that may occur. First of all, the grant of a right of option under a treaty agreed between the parties to a state succession, and possibly other states as well who have an interest in the matter; and secondly, it can come into existence by the passing of appropriate national legislation. Those are the two ways in which a right of option can be created.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, but there is a nuance that should be brought out here. That is, international treaties were used in the past, that was the way that right of option was provided for, that is in treaties, which regulated all cases dealing with state succession, but the treaties always provided for an option between two things. There was a dilemma, nationality of the successor state or nationality of the predecessor state. After the Second World War, there were option rights that were granted through national laws, it was not that one was to choose between nationalities, but there was only one option. For example look at my own nationality. It has to do with the nationality of the state passing laws, but I do agree with you that in both cases we have got a right of option, but in the first case, this is to choose between two nationalities, in the second case it is to choose one nationality which has been determined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Venice Commission, I think it was, that sent round a questionnaire to its various member states asking it for examples of instances of state succession and what had happened on those occasions. I think you drafted the reply on behalf of your country to that questionnaire, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your evidence about the existence of the possibility of rights of option, you went through the experience of your country over quite a number of years, and occasions when rights of option had been granted. Just by way of example, I would like, if we may, Professor, please, to just go through those instances. First of all, can you just help me about this? I think in Greek law, there is no possibility of people holding multiple nationality, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not quite right. According to Greek law, there is Greek nationality, of course, but there are many Greeks who have dual nationality. Actually, even Greece, which has many Greeks outside its own borders, is a country which favours the idea of dual nationality, even multiple nationalities. All Greeks who are in the United States, there are about three million of them, are Greeks and also citizens of the United States, that is US nationals. The same thing applies to those Greeks in Australia or in Canada or throughout the world. Therefore as far as nationality goes, Greece has a very flexible approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment, please? (Pause). I asked that question, Professor, because the forms which have been created setting out the various examples in relation to Greece indicate that multiple nationality was not a possibility, but plainly that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that you are right, it was pointed out by the Secretariat of Europe, but this was an error, and I am sure that you saw that error and you thought it was correct. But there were mistakes that had been made in the reports of the Council of Europe. No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am glad to know they are not infallible. Professor, help me about this. The first time I think that a right of option was granted by your country was in 1881 upon the incorporation, and you will forgive me for mispronouncing the names of parts of your country, I am sure, Thessaly and parts of Epiros in 1881.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Epiros, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please forgive me for massacring your language. It is not one I can do. Then the second occasion was 1913 when Macedonia, Crete and some islands in the Aegean were incorporated into Greece?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next was between 1919 and 1923 when Western Thrace was incorporated into Greece.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final occasion was 1947 when the islands, the Dodecanes, were again incorporated into Greece?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was one aspect of each of those grants of right of option that had rather dramatic consequences for those who chose to exercise the right of option; in other words, if you chose to exercise the right of option, I think on each occasion except for one -- twice it was a right to retain Ottoman nationality, Western Thrace it was an option to retain Bulgarian nationality and the Dodecanes Italian, but you had to leave the territory, did you not? If you chose to exercise your right, you had to leave your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The obligation to quit that territory, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is right. That was a fairly drastic consequence of the exercise of a right of option.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it is a consequence which has been very common when rights of option have been granted, it has been frequently accompanied by the state granting the right of option insisting that those who exercise it must leave the territory. Would you agree with this, Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree absolutely with you and this is why: in the Venice Commission, we try to change that rule, rather that practice, and we stated in Article 6 that the option favouring the predecessor state must not have prejudicial consequences for those who are obtaining them, specifically as regards their right to reside on the territory of the successor state, and as their property, whether real or moveable, that is one is trying to change the rule and I do agree with you that in former times, we experienced a practice which I can say was relatively inhuman, because what is the right of option if you choose the nationality of the successor state, you have to then leave and take all your property, you have to disappear from the successor state. This is really a very violent way of approaching things. That is why we are trying to change the rule which in fact was applied until the end of the Second World War. Yes, I agree absolutely with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me about this: since 1990, within those states which reported -- answered the questionnaire as you did, I think there were a total of 15 occasions since 1990 when a succession of states had taken place, and of those, eight had granted a right of option, but six had not granted a right of option. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that I really did not count the cases, but I know that the right of options were not granted in all cases. This more or less confirms what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the rough similarity of figures, it appears that state practice is somewhat divided at the present time as to the obligation to grant a right of option.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think this has to be said with some nuance. The former practice was much stronger. There was no doubt at all that the right of option was very current, but with the serious consequences which you have just pointed out. After the Second World War, the rights of option still appear, but they were not always respected in all cases. You know that international law has a great many weak points, and is not always honoured, but that is another issue, that is another chapter that I do not want to get into here. There are flaws in international law that are well known by everybody, violations of international law which are never punished, but this does not mean that international law does not exist and that the obligation does not exist, even if it is not honoured in all cases. But I would say now that I do not really remember in which cases rights were granted and which cases they were not. That is all I wanted to say about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not want to go through a long list of states which have and have not granted rights of option, otherwise we will be here for a great length of time. Help me about this, Professor. Let us assume that either by treaty or by legislation a right of option is in fact granted. If a right of option has been granted to the citizens, to the nationals of a country, there has to be some formal act in order to exercise that option, does there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, a form has to be filled out applying for that nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the state whose nationality has been applied for will have to give out, for example, a certificate of nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suspect that in pretty well every country in the world there is an obligation to swear an oath of allegiance to the state of which you have applied for nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot simply wake up one morning, for example in 1913, and say to yourself, "I feel Ottoman this morning".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in general there are certain rules. At least a piece of paper must be signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely so. You told us on the last occasion that you had not looked into the question of what the nationality laws of the states of the former Yugoslavia were, but as far as you know, there was no grant of a right of option in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. In the absence of a grant of a right of option, it was not possible for the habitual residents of that territory to opt for some other nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is right, is it not, that Bosnia-Herzegovina was pretty prompt in passing a nationality law, I think the day following its declaration of independence; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. I think that I had heard about a nationality law in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was in October 1992, whereas independence had occurred well before that, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We need not go into the detail of that, but you are satisfied no right of option was granted to the habitual residents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so effectively they became citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina upon the succession of states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a very important question. Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes an independent state in 1992, I believe it was in April. No laws were passed, whereas ordinarily, new states first and foremost, before anything else, it seems to me, do that, whereas Bosnia-Herzegovina did not do that at all, which means by interpretation that Bosnia-Herzegovina maintained its previous law having to do with nationality, which is a law which had been passed as part of the former Yugoslavia and the law remained in effect, it was not rescinded, there were no other ones, therefore one must assume that the previous law remained in force, whereas that previous law stated that all Bosnians are concomitantly nationals of Yugoslavia. Therefore I must say that we have to accept that for a certain amount of time all Bosnians had dual nationality, the nationality of the former Yugoslavia and the nationality of Bosnia-Herzegovina, pursuant to the law of 1900 I do not know what, which had been passed as part of the former Yugoslavia. Therefore I agree with you and say that they were all Bosnians, but at the same time they were also nationals of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is in April 1992. Therefore there was dual nationality for everybody in my opinion, as an interpreter of the facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are just going to come to the break, but one last question on this topic, Professor. As you have agreed before, at the moment of dissolution of the former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, that nationality ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that a convenient moment, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break and reassemble at 12.00. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly invite the witness, please? (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours may be pleased to hear that I have no further questions for the professor. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I guess it is good afternoon, your Honour. May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may continue, please. Cross-examined by MR. MORAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good afternoon, Professor. My name is Tom Moran and I am an attorney, I represent a man named Hazim Delic. I am going to ask you a few questions having to do with some of the things you testified about earlier today and also to clarify in my mind, and hopefully in the court's mind some of the questions that were posed to you by members of the court, and if there is any question I ask that is not clear to you, will you please stop me and have me clear it up. Let me start with this, Professor. Would you agree with me that there are basically four sources of international law, and those would be the four sources that are listed in Article 38 of the Statute of the ICJ; international conventions, whether general or particular, expressing rules expressly recognised by the contesting states; international custom as evidence of a general practice accepted as law; three, the general principles of law recognised by civilised nations; four, judicial decisions and teachings of the most highly qualified publicists of the various nations, as a subsidiary means for the determination of the rules of law. Would you agree with me that those are the sources of international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree absolutely with you, but I would like to also say that the first three sources are the main sources and the last, that is legal opinion, is an auxiliary source.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me and I am going to show you two sets of books, one is Oppenheim's International Law, edited by Sir Robert Jennings, and the other is Principles of Public International Law, by Ian Brownlie. Would you agree with me that both of those are authoritative as to the laws of international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More than references, they really are authorities, scientific authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact since Sir Robert Jennings was the President of the World Court, I do not think any of us would disagree that he probably has a feeling for international law. Also I want to talk to you a little bit just in general about the ILC reports, including the one -- actually it was two, from 12th to 18th July this year, and I believe it is United Nations document number A5/2/10 and then there was an appendix -- actually I have another United Nations number, A/CN.4/480. That is the one that has -- that was published 27th February of this year and there was another one, A/CN.4/480/add 1 from the next day, which is a report of nationality in relation to succession of states by Mr. Michael of the special rapporteur. Would you agree with me that those set forth what had occurred in your meetings at the ILC? You had a chance to read those documents before they were published as General Assembly documents, and if you thought that there was something wrong with them, you could have changed them or put in a dissenting opinion or something like that, could you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did read all these documents. I do not have them with me, of course, but I read them a long time ago, and I must say that the report of the special rapporteur is a document which really has authority, but it does not mean that the texts that we adopted afterwards always reflect the positions which appear in the report. What has much more credibility, much more authority, is the report itself and less the report of the special rapporteur, which is very extensive and which is not in all cases followed by the International Law Commission, but I do agree with you that in these reports there are many more details having to do with the issue that is under review today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also I want to talk to you about the Venice Commission report. I have got several of them, I am just going to talk about them in general with you right now. I have one dated 10th February and there is one dated 13th to 14th September 1996. You were involved in the preparation of those, were you not, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could have suggested changes or if you thought that they did something absolutely wrong, you could have issued a dissenting opinion, could you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those are authoritative also, both as to the facts and to the proposals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. With that said, would you also agree with me that the Appellate Chamber of this Tribunal has the competence and the jurisdiction to interpret and decide what is international law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, within the scope of this jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, I will be real frank with you. I was going over your testimony from October 30th, and then I listened to your testimony here today, and frankly, I was a little confused about some things. So I am going to ask you to help me clear some of these things up. Some of them I think you already have. Judge Karibi-Whyte asked this question, it had to do with a war situation and an occupation, and I believe your response to Judge Karibi-Whyte was that an occupier cannot change nationality, that is a matter of international humanitarian law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. An occupying state which by force is occupying a territory cannot change the nationality. The military occupation cannot change either the sovereignty which falls under the state which is militarily occupied or the status of the person residing on that territory. Therefore military occupation does not change nationality. Greece was occupied by Germany during the Second World War for four years. Greece did not become a German territory, and the Greeks did not change their nationality to become German nationals. Therefore that does not fall within our field of application, and I repeat once again, a military occupation does not change the sovereignty or the sovereignty of the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In fact that is The Hague Convention of 1970 that sets out that as international law, is that correct? On the other hand, as part of a war, sovereignty over land can be transferred. One example that comes to mind is Alsace-Lorraine, that has probably changed between France and Germany, what, three times in the last 100 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happens, but this goes through peace treaties which settle war questions, which create the peace conditions and regulate the whole issue. The war itself as an event does not change the question, but peace which is agreed upon by the different states who were involved in the war, that can -- the treaty can change the situation and settle things in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, someone just handed me a note and I am usually pretty good about this and I frankly missed it. If you look around the courtroom, you see two ladies, one over there and one over there, the court reporters. They have to write down everything we say. They cannot write down a nod and you have been nodding. If you would answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you have a change -- Alsace-Lorraine, we will pick on Alsace for a minute. When there is a treaty of peace between France and Germany, the treaty can say these people become citizens of Germany or citizens of France.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that way, a war can change nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through a peace treaty, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or a victor can just annex the territory, can he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Formerly, in the very beginnings of international law that was accepted, but since then and since the First World War and especially so since the Second World War, force was ruled out altogether, recourse to force is an illegal act and unilateral annexation is something irregular which should trigger security measures by the Security Council of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We can have several ways that sovereignty over people and territory can change. We can have a secession from a state, right? Some portion of a country leaves another country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, based on the self-determination law, that is the normal course of things. The self-determination right is exerted by specific states which can become independent based on that law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can also have states joining together to become one state. In fact, one of the examples that you used in the Venice Commission report is one that I am very familiar with, just because of where I am from, the annexation of the republic of Texas by the United States in 1845. It is one of the specific examples you used. In that case, one nation ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So its nationality ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is quite valid. You have a recent case with Germany, of both Germanys that merge into one state. There is an union of states then, but initially there was an international treaty settling all those matters and they became operational later, but indeed the union of states is a very well accepted manner in international law which triggers change in nationality, but that happens in times of peace and not through recourse to illegal force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And another way that you can have a change in sovereignty is a nation essentially explodes and the example I will use of that is the Soviet Union in 1991 ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there again there was a dissolution treaty, that was signed and the former Soviet Union exploded altogether, but on the basis of a prior treaty which established or which provided for the dissolution and the explosion, as such, of the former Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us use the Soviet union as an example and talk about international law, about that. We all remember back in December 1991 President Gorbachev making a speech and resigning and essentially at that point the Soviet Union ceased to exist; we can agree on that, can we not, as an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the Soviet Union ceased to exist as of the time when the treaty was signed in the capital of Belarus that provided for the dissolution of the Soviet empire. Was that not in 1992? I do not have the dates with me, I did not look into this more specifically, but I know that then we had a treaty that provided for the dissolution of the Soviet Union. From that moment, from the time when the treaty was signed, do we have the dissolution? It is not Gorbachev's speech as such that put an end to the Soviet Union, it is the treaty. I fail to remember the name of the capital, but it is as of that time and through that treaty that it became a reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any case, under international law, no matter how much you or I would want to be a citizen of the Soviet Union today, we cannot do that, right, because the Soviet Union no longer exists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So under international law, each of the constituent republics of the former Soviet Union had an obligation to grant citizenship in the Ukraine or Belarus, or wherever, to all habitual residents of that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to prevent statelessness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there is a right of choice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That does not mean that if I were a habitual resident of the Ukraine and the Soviet Union ceased to exist, I could say, "I exercise my right of choice, I want to be a citizen of the United Kingdom", does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
