In this Chamber, as early as 2nd April, during the testimony of Stevan Gligorevic, the Defence of Mr. Delalic requested that Mr. Gligorevic provide a sample signature for analysis when he claimed that a signature on a document was not his. Of course, your Honours, more specifically, and on point to the matter today, we have the transcript of 10th June 1997, portions of which are reproduced in our response. Your Honours have gone through that and have read it and I will not dwell on it but it is clear both from the cross-examination of Officer Moerbauer by Madam Residovic and the comments of Judge Jan to Mr. Turone that the Prosecution was alerted to the issue of proving documents strictly by handwriting analysis. Your Honours, we respectfully submit that the timing of this motion shows that the Prosecution has been dilatory in the extreme in dealing with this issue. The Prosecution has had six months since June in which to obtain such evidence. Their failure to seek to adduce this evidence in a timely fashion is clearly contrary to both the letter and the spirit of your order. It is respectfully submitted that the Prosecution cannot say, as they say in their motion, that this issue has only recently arisen. Aside from the foregoing, the Prosecution is well aware of the rules of evidence and the decisions of this court, and I am thinking specifically of Rule 89 and Tadic, which have been argued many times before you and I will not repeat what has already been said, but your Honours again, for the Prosecution to say with the knowledge that they have been alerted by your Honours, being aware of the rules and the case law, there is no good cause shown and no justification for this late attempt at calling this witness. As has already been stated in the exchange between your Honours and Mr. Niemann, we went through submissions, full submissions by both sides, the Prosecution and the Defence in our last sitting in late October/early November. Full submissions were made by both sides as to the admissibility of these questioned documents. These submissions, I hasten to add, again were made with the full knowledge of the Prosecution of comments from the bench in June, what the rules of this Tribunal are and what the case law of this Tribunal also holds as precursors to proving evidence. For these reasons, your Honours, it is submitted that granting leave to call Ms Stegnar should be denied. The Prosecution has not shown good cause or provided justification. The record of the trial demonstrates that no good cause or justification exists and in his oral submissions, Mr. Niemann has provided none either. We say that the calling of this witness would deny Mr. Delalic, for these reasons, the right to a fair trial. If I can briefly address you on the second issue we raise in our response, which is that if in the event your Honours grant the request to call the witness, we submit that the timetable proposed by the Prosecution is unjust and unfair. The Prosecution has indicated they wish to call their expert this week. I have made submissions on the effect of the untimely nature of this request, but all those matters as well apply to the proposed timetable. I should like first of all to draw your attention to three documents which are connected with this matter and that is the letter my friend referred to of November 18th, their motion of November 20th and an expert report which we received last Friday, 28th November. Let me begin by pointing out, your Honours, that the report by their handwriting expert is dated November 26th, and in spite of that, it was received by the Defence at 3.45 last Friday afternoon, the 28th. Contrary to the assertions contained in the Prosecution motion, for all intents and purposes, this is the first time we have seen the content of what this witness's testimony may be; that is late last Friday afternoon. The Prosecution had claimed that we had received the content in the letter of 18th November, but in my respectful submission that is quite incorrect. All the letter of the 18th states is that their witness has made a preliminary assessment of some, not all documents and that her report would be given to us by last Friday at the latest. Furthermore, and contrary to what the Prosecution has claimed, we have not had two weeks to prepare a cross-examination of this witness. Again, I repeat that only last Friday did we receive their expert's report. We did manage to contact an expert, but like any busy professional who is competent, it is not easy for a person on such short notice to be free to be here to conduct a proper response and an analysis of documents and to contemplate what the Prosecution expert has said. This is important if we are to prepare a cross-examination on a technical expertise, one which is beyond the normal scope of counsel. We need assistance if in fact this woman is to testify. Further, your Honours, pursuant to Rule 90 of our Rules, the Defence would like to have its expert present during the testimony of the expert witness for the Prosecution, if she should testify. As your Honours know, Rule 90 deals with testimony of witnesses, and the relevant portion of that rule for this matter is the first sentence, which reads as follows: "A witness, other than an expert who has not yet testified, shall not be present when the testimony of another witness is given." Clearly, your Honours, this rule contemplates the presence of one party's expert during the testimony of the other party's expert, an interpretation which is clearly gleaned from the language of Rule 90 and also from your decision of 20th March 1997 on the question of allowing investigators to follow proceedings. The point here, your Honours, is that should you allow the Prosecution expert to testify -- the point, your Honour, is, should you allow the Prosecution witness to testify, we would like our expert to be present during her testimony, but again, because of the timing of this Prosecution application, because of the late receipt of their report, it is impossible for our expert to be free to be here this week because of previous professional and personal obligations. Finally, in regard to cross-examination generally, it is in my respectful submission inappropriate for the Prosecution to think that they can determine on behalf of the Defence whether a witness should be classified broadly or narrowly, in detail or in general, as they have done in their motion. The Prosecution has attempted to call this expert at the eleventh hour in this case and then seeks to rush the Defence. I hasten to add that during the nine months that the Prosecution has been presenting its case, they appeared to be in no hurry and no pressure was exerted on them to hurry. We submit that this arrogation to themselves about the manner in which Defence should cross-examine again is ample example of the indifference of the defendant's right in this matter. We respectfully submit that should your Honours grant leave to call the Prosecution's expert, the proposed timetable is unfair and hopelessly unrealistic. To conclude, your Honours, I should like to add the following observations in relation to this matter and I make them generally in support of my preceding submissions and I shall be brief. It seems that there is a certain flavour to this motion by the Prosecution which is troubling both in tone and content. In its motion, the Prosecution attempts to underpin its request by making certain comments on the nature of this exercise. They appear to describe this trial as a truth seeking process. With all due respect, might I point out that the Prosecution seems to have forgotten that we are involved in a criminal Prosecution. It is therefore for the Prosecution to prove their case against the accused who throughout the process must benefit from the presumption of innocence and against whom the standard of proof throughout the case is, in my respectful submission, beyond reasonable doubt. The burden of reasonable doubt has been confirmed by this Chamber in its decision excluding the Mucic statement made to the Viennese police. Your Honours have responded to a clarification request by Delalic by saying that the Prosecution must prove all elements of its case. In relation to the Viennese documents the Prosecution has recognised and admitted that they have been put to strict proof. The Prosecution also seems bothered, your Honours, by rules of evidence which it qualifies as highly restrictive evidentiary standards which would vitiate the spirit of the Statute of this Tribunal. That is the language they use in their motion. Here, your Honours, the Prosecution is effectively saying that the principles for admissibility of documents which we say are predicated by the Tadic decision on hearsay are highly restrictive evidentiary standards, when in fact they are no more than the common sense set of principles which put flesh on the bones of Rule 89. It will not have escaped your Honours' notice that the Prosecution seems to habitually either ignore or attempt to evade the Rules and decisions of this Tribunal. This instance is just another striking example of that tendency, in my submission. We note moreover that in its motion, the Prosecution sets much store in, and I quote, "the spirit of the Statute of the Tribunal, as well as the legitimate expectations of the victims of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and the international community." We respectfully submit that it might be appropriate to recall some aspects of the Statute in order to properly assess the spirit of the Statute. Again, this is a criminal Tribunal, whose primary objective must be to do justice to the accused. We submit that Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute are the two provisions which best define the spirit of our Statute, in particular Articles 20(1), 21(2), 21(3) and 21(4)(b). In our respectful submission, these articles should be read in this regard in conjunction with three Rules, 87, 89 and 95. Your Honours, the spirit of the Statute, as it concerns these matters, lays stress on the granting of a fair trial to the defendant, in accordance with the Rules, and his right to be given a proper time to prepare his Defence. As I pointed out a moment ago, what the Prosecution is prompted to describe as highly restrictive evidentiary standards are no more than the common sense principles of the Tadic decision. Those principles are, in our submission, a fine example of how this honourable Tribunal seeks to implement the spirit of the Statute on guaranteeing fair trial provisions. Your Honours, let us not forget that while we accept entirely that part of the process of this trial which involves constant consideration of the interests of the many victims of serious violence in the former Yugoslavia, we respectfully point out that there is nothing in the Statute or the Rules that suggests that either the spirit or the letter of those provisions is to allow those interests in any way to override those set out in Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute. As for the legitimate expectations of the international community, we submit that the Statute itself is a written embodiment of what those expectations are, it having been agreed to by the UN, and namely those are that the accused person will get a fair trial. If the Prosecution asserts that those expectations are different, we would invite them to spell out unambiguously what those expectations are. In summary, therefore, we say the Prosecution has failed to make this application in good time, has not shown good cause or justification for calling this witness or reopening this issue. In the alternative, if granted, this honourable Tribunal should not accede to the proposed timetable of the Prosecution, because that timetable would act unjustly upon the rights and interests of the accused. Those are my submissions on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Firstly, your Honour, I find it extraordinarily upsetting that counsel chooses to make suggestions like, "the Prosecution is evading or ignoring decisions and Rules of this Tribunal". It is a most regrettable approach that counsel seems to take, and why they feel it necessary to do so is beyond me, but I call upon them to give us yet one example of where that is the case. But to deal with the matters raised other than that, there is no arrogation by the Prosecution of limitation of the cross-examination of a witness. It is a matter for your Honours to determine how long someone will be cross-examined for. The point is that the Defence would have you believe that in order for them to have a fair trial, they are to have unlimited, unrestricted cross-examination which will go on for as long as they deem appropriate, all in the name of a fair trial. This, in my submission, clearly demonstrates a misunderstanding on their part of what a fair trial is. A fair trial is the division between one party and the other of the rights and benefits of presenting a case, and that the Defence should not be disadvantaged in any way where the Prosecution is not disadvantaged, but it is a two way street, and it is not something that is in the exclusive domain of the Defence. The giving of a fair trial is a balancing act. They forget one side of the scales. Your Honours, with respect to having their expert present, they have a transcript, the transcript can be examined, they have a report, that report can be examined. It is not beyond the wit of a competent expert to have regard to that and respond to it, so if for whatever reason their expert could not be here today, and we have not heard of reasons why the expert cannot be here today, other than just could not make it because of other commitments, but it seems to me, your Honours, that the presence of the expert is not necessary for that purpose, in any event. Your Honours, counsel seems to dispute that this is a truth seeking process. If it is not a truth seeking process, then I do not know what it is, because in my submission, your Honours, it is only by a search for the truth that a true determination can be made as to the guilt or innocence of the accused. Your Honours, we have a copy of the letter here that we gave to the Defence, because they place such emphasis on the fact that they only have got the report on Friday. We told them in the letter that we would have the report for them by Friday, but it was on 18th November that we gave them substantial detail on this matter and I hand it to your Honours. I only have one copy, I am afraid, your Honours. (Handed). In our submission, your Honours, this application is fairly and properly based, having regard to the decision that your Honours made in relation to the Mucic document --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object to this letter between counsel being handed to the bench. I do not see this as an appropriate path for counsel to follow at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is the letter sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your objection, if it was sent to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour should not be seeing the content of the letter. My friend is saying it contains information on the expert's views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not see the basis for your objection. If the letter was sent to you and it is being shown to the Trial Chamber, I do not see why you should not want the Trial Chamber to see the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I do not see for what reason he would want to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond, he was the one that raised it and he was the one that said it did not provide them with sufficient information and tried to argue that it was only the report that they received on Friday. If he raises it then so be it, but your Honour, we are entitled to respond and to demonstrate to you that we gave them ample notice of what they could expect to find from this expert witness in plenty of time for them to prepare. He knew, and I said when I made my submissions, that we deliberately did not give you this letter because it contained the preliminary conclusions. We believed it would be unfair. If he then gets up and makes submissions about the fact that we have not given them sufficient notice of things, then, your Honours, this is what they must expect in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With all due respect, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was after they said that we evade decisions of the Tribunal, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, reference to this letter is to show the time-frame and the short fuse with which we were given notice, not because of the content of the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are still complaining about the dates, that the time was too short, but that does not mean that the Trial Chamber should not see a letter written to you in anticipation of what is coming before the Trial Chamber. There is nothing wrong with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In response to my friend Mr. Niemann, I am just saying that the reason I made reference to the letter, the reports and the motion was to show the dates, not the content. That is the point I am making. I say the relevancy of all this is the dates and the time-frames.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is the 18th you mentioned, and that is the date of the letter. This is not a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But the contents of the letter is not appropriate for the point I made to you, your Honours. I was talking about the dates, not the contents of those letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nothing should be shut out of the Trial Chamber, if it is relevant to the issue before it. The area of one's observation is quite different, not whether letters have been written to you. It is quite a different consideration. Have you concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will come back by 4.30. Then we will give our decision. (3.55 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We are trying to read a very short ruling. The application before us is by the Prosecution for leave to call an expert witness. The Prosecution and Defence had concluded their submissions on an application of the Prosecution to tender into evidence certain exhibits on 31st October 1997. The Prosecution has now brought this motion for leave to call this expert witness in respect of the documents. Although Prosecution has indicated the evidence of the expert will concern only Mr. Delalic, the exhibits which require the evidence of the expert are not indicated in the motion. Counsel for the Prosecution in the arguments has informed the Trial Chamber that a letter has been written to the Defence indicating the documents affected. Counsel to Mr. Delalic is opposing the motion. Among the grounds relied upon, some which are substantive, is that the Prosecution has not shown good cause or justifiable reason for the application. It was also submitted that the Prosecution has not given the Defence adequate notice to prepare for the testimony of the expert. It is admitted that the Prosecution has sent a preliminary of the expert to the Defence, but the Defence regard this as insufficient for the preparation of the expert's testimony. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the Prosecution has not shown good cause why leave should be granted for them to reopen the matter after parties had made their final submission in respect of the tendering of those documents. The reason given about caution because of a recent ruling by itself is not good cause. The expert has not been shown to be unavailable before now, or that the reason for his being invited was not in existence. The issue of the possibility of proof of these documents has always been known to the Prosecution several months ago. The Trial Chamber is therefore not satisfied that the Defence has been given sufficient notice to prepare for the evidence of the expert, and we do not consider it in the interests of justice to give the leave sought. We do not think it is necessary to go into the other reasons for the opposition to the application. The motion is therefore refused. I think this is our ruling on the matter. I think you have another motion, have you? If you have any other motion, we will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just bring up two logistical issues, they are not new motions but in preparation for closing our case. I want to -- the Registrar has indicated that I should in open court proffer the video excerpts that were shown to Witness T. They previously have been shown from the original, and then I was subsequently instructed that there should be excerpts of what was shown and identified to the witness separated from the originals. That has been done, so just in open court, so we can have the numbers, I wish to proffer them. They already have been identified as part of the testimony. Obviously if Defence wishes they can later verify that they are in fact the excerpts identified by Witness T, but if I may just do that and get the numbers in open court, that is the first issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I wish I understood any of the things you have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour, let me start again. Witness T previously testified. Witness T was an employee at the Celebici camp. Using the original tapes, he was shown excerpts from the tapes and he identified them. I was then instructed that an excerpted video, just showing the parts that the witness identified, should be prepared to make it easier for everyone, including the court, the Defence and the Prosecution, to know exactly what the witness was shown and identified. I believe this has been done previously but I am not exactly -- I know the Defence has done it too, I do not know whether or not they have always been given separate numbers, but in this case at least, I was told that we should do this in open court just so that the numbers could be reflected in open court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The videos are prepared by Witness T himself?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What this is is just the excerpts of what the witness saw and said "yes, I was present or I took this", whatever. (Handed). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Was the Defence aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I believe, and it had been agreed with the Defence that this would be done. Of course, I have no objection if they later on want to verify --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is part of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the Defence said only the excerpts should be exhibited, not the entire videos.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So you have prepared the excerpts and now you want to present them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to some extent I can verify that and additionally say that just before we started the afternoon session, Ms McHenry informed me she was going to make this offer. It seems to me that it really would be a great deal more helpful in terms of making sure we are not on different pages here, they have apparently had these excerpts for a long time, to simply give us a tape and say "these are the excerpts we think are appropriate out of Witness T's testimony, take a look at it. If you have any objection, let us know and we will get it cleaned up". Obviously we have not had a chance to look at the tapes that were made and I am confident we will have a chance to do that and if we have any later objection, the Chamber will hear it, but it seems like a more logical way to do it, if they want to do something like this, to give us a copy of the excerpts and say "these are the ones we think are appropriate", rather than make us go through this process of raising the matter at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It has been done at your own request that only the excerpts that had been shown to the witness should be exhibited, so the other material from the tape was taken off and these excerpts were prepared separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not making any objection whatsoever, it is just a suggestion to make things work a little more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose this is a matter of co-operation between the Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for that very reason, perhaps we could clear up some other questions too. The Prosecution probably has some other excerpts shown during the testimony, so that perhaps all the others should be treated in the same way. I draw attention to the fact that some documents that we are discussing include tapes, entire tapes, so it would be a good idea to include in the evidence only the excerpt that corresponds to the excerpt shown to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I do not have terribly much to say, but if my learned friend Ms McHenry asserts to me that those are the excerpts she showed to the witness, I will, of course, accept it. If it turns out they are not, I will telephone her.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just have the numbers for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: These excerpts are from videotapes which have been already marked as Prosecutor's Exhibits 110, 111 and 112. So they will be marked 110C, 111C and 112C.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the next matter, entirely unrelated, again as part of preparing to close our case, it was brought to our attention with respect to the testimony of Ms. Milojka Antic, who testified that she had been raped in the Celebici camp, and the Defence impeached her -- attempted to impeach her on numerous occasions about her prior statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. It has come to our attention that that statement was not offered at the time of her testimony, but because it was referred to on numerous occasions, the Prosecution, as it has stated, we have had this same argument and discussion before, believes it appropriate for your Honours to have her statement, only to determine the extent to which she has been impeached. We do not offer it as substantive evidence, only as it relates to her credibility, as to which she is impeached. I have extra copies for both the Chamber and Defence counsel and obviously Defence counsel previously has this, but I would just offer these into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the limited nature of the offer, that if they are not offered for the truth of the matter asserted therein --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I was saying, given the limited nature, I will have no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 209.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I believe that would have been the normal course in my country also. Your Honours, that is all the matters we have to bring forward for you now. With your Honours' ruling, we have no additional witnesses for this week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we have before us here your motion to dismiss counts 40 and 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am sure the Defence will not object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. If you wish we will speak to it, but I believe it speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Has the Defence any views on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Moran will probably be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have not seen the motion, but any time the Prosecution wishes to dismiss a count against my client -- I would like to ask them to dismiss a few more, but I do not think they will do it. I have no objection to them dismissing anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The motion to dismiss is granted. In the absence of any other thing, I think we will take the opportunity to assess where we all are now and what we should come back to do in January. I know you have all indicated you will keep cross-examining Dr. Gow, and apart from him, I see no other evidence before the Trial Chamber. So after that, it is left to the Defence to tell us how you will go, how things are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall that we had discussed earlier and there had been agreement between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence regarding the preparation and filing of a motion to dismiss at the close of the Prosecution's case. My expectation, and I do not want to be held to this, but my expectation is that we will finish with Dr. Gow, if we are coming back on January 12th, which is my understanding, that Dr. Gow would go back on the witness stand that day, that we would finish with Dr. Gow probably on 13th January. What we had discussed previously is once the Prosecution has rested, that there would be a period of two weeks for us to prepare and file our motions to dismiss, that the Prosecution would then have two weeks to respond, followed by a week for us to respond; then as soon as the Trial Chamber makes its ruling, we were prepared then to go forward with the Defence case. That is our view of how we should go from this point. I think it is the unanimous view of all my colleagues along the table here, I see nobody saying no, and you will recall that earlier the Office of the Prosecutor, when we brought this matter up before, had agreed that that would be a fair way to do it. I assume they have not changed their position, but I am certain they will tell you if they have. That is what we would request and that is what we would hope can happen next in the case. The process of preparing this motion is underway, but it is as you can imagine with I think maybe as much as 9,000 pages of transcript to deal with at this point, it is not an easy task. There are some significant legal issues and it is something we just need to have some rather unencumbered time to get worked through. We are going to try to file a joint motion, we are hoping we can do that. If that is not possible, then we will perhaps file a joint motion as to some of the issues and separate motions as to some of the issues, but we are going to try to get through it as quickly as we can and I think two weeks is a reasonable request in that regard. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Mr. Ackerman, the cross-examination of Dr. Gow will finish you said on 13th; your cross-examination, or for the whole cross-examination or only your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the best I can tell you, and it is impossible to predict, as you could see, Dr. Gow sometimes likes to give longer answers than one would expect, but I would think that what I have left with Dr. Gow I could do in a day or a little bit less. I am not sure how long other counsel have, I think I can be reasonably safe saying that we would finish some time that Tuesday 13th, of everybody, all cross-examinations I think would finish on that day. I cannot imagine that anyone else would take as long as I will take, because I intend to cover virtually everything that anybody might have in mind. It may be that someone else would have a few questions, but I am reasonably certain we would finish on the 13th. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: That is what I thought. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have heard the examination-in-chief of Dr. Gow, we have also heard part of the cross-examination, maybe this period of December you can utilise in preparing your motion, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all of us will be utilising this period of time at least to some extent in preparing that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It should be ready in January when we have finished with Dr. Gow's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me tell the Trial Chamber this, and I think it is important. It is awfully important to me and some other people. That period of time that will run from now until early January, a significant portion of that very many of us on this side of the room have made significant plans to be with our families. It is a holiday period that is important to many of us. I have plans to spend a significant portion of that time with my mother, who is getting quite along in years in Arizona. I have not seen her for quite a long time. I know that others of us have plans to be with our family during that time. It is a time when ordinarily we set aside to spend with our families. It is more important perhaps for many of us this year than in other years, because we have been spending an extraordinary amount of our time sitting in The Hague being away from our families. So we would just hope -- I understand the need to move forward with the case, I understand that the whole -- this whole building would like us to finish this case as quickly as possible, but on the other hand, I think that holiday period is important, perhaps more important than the considerations that might go into how quickly we finish this case. It is certainly not -- we certainly will not have the opportunity, because some of us simply will not abandon those plans, to do the kind of work that is necessary to accomplish what your Honour is suggesting. I cannot take with me all of the exhibits and the entire transcript of this case, wherever I go in the world. It is just too much, I would need a truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can have a CD ROM, you can have all evidence on a small disk, 3.5 inches thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not know how I can do that, your Honour. If somebody could show me a way to do that, I would be happy. In any event, there is really a lot of work that needs to be done jointly with us all here together to try to accomplish this in a reasonable manner. I think two weeks is not a long time to ask for that, considering the amount of material that we have to work with. We will all be doing a great deal of that work during the time we are on holiday, but it is not something we can work at jointly and together and in an organised manner. I would be surprised if members of the Office of the Prosecutor do not have the same kind of plans regarding family activities during those holidays. It is fairly traditional for a lot of us. For some of us, of course, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, along that line Mr. Ackerman pointed out to the court that the process is already in progress. I have written a substantial portion and then rewrote it, cut it down, rather than -- writing short, believe me, is harder than writing long. To try to cut down the number of words that I am going to -- to deliver to the Trial Chamber. I do not want to give you something I have to bring in on a wheelbarrow and I do not think the Trial Chamber would like us to do that. Just those kinds of things require a lot of work, we want to be able to sit down, the Defence counsel together, and say, "okay, this is it, this is the package that we have to work from", go through 8,000 or 9,000 pages of testimony and try and get something that presents the legal and factual issues to the Trial Chamber in frankly as short a manner as possible. At the same time, I think that the Prosecution, to be fair to them, they should have been thinking about these issues all along and they are probably anticipating some of the things we are going to say, and they need to have that document sitting on their desk, to be fair to the Prosecutor, so again the issues can be clearly drawn in a reasonable manner for the Trial Chamber. I think we are going to require some time after the close of the Prosecutor's case. I do not think the Prosecutor could say "we rest" and then we reach down in our briefcases and hand something to the Trial Chamber. I do not think that is something we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you been thinking about the projection of your witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So that we might know exactly how things might unfold as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have discussed it among ourselves, both as individuals, who is going to call what witnesses, the order we are going to go in. In fact, I was going to ask for some guidance at some point from the Trial Chamber on (i) what order do you want to see the Defence, and (ii), just as a technical thing, on how we should proceed on cross-examination. I can tell you what the practice is in multiple defendant trials where I have been before. During the Defence case, which would be first, there is a direct examination, one defendant calls a witness, there is a direct examination, followed by cross-examination by the Prosecutor, followed then by cross-examination by the other defendants. That is the procedure that I have seen, I would ask the Trial Chamber to adopt that, but I think it is something we need to think about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is usually a practice where Defence counsel agree among themselves in areas where they might not even cross-examine, before it starts. It makes life easier for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree with your Honour. If those kinds of things -- I am sure that to take some of them at random, Mr. Delalic is likely to call some witnesses that are going to have absolutely nothing to do with Mr. Delic, and I am not going to have anything to say to those witnesses. But I think those are the kinds of technical things that we need to be thinking about prior to the start of the Defence case. I know that Mr. Karabdic has been working very hard talking to witnesses in the former Yugoslavia, preparing to provide the Victim and Witnesses Unit with locations and various other information that they need so that we can do this in some kind of a rational --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because of the nature of our facilities here, and for the purpose of arrangement of Trial Chambers, it is fairly necessary for us to know exactly the size of the Defence case so that we will know what to do in determining how long we could take, one week, two weeks, because if you have a fair idea of how many witnesses are likely to be involved, then we will know for how long it will take and a fair estimate of how much the cross-examination will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would expect and I am begging you not to hold me to this, I am expecting that over the holidays, I will probably -- we will discuss it and there will probably be, what, ten to fifteen fact witnesses, is that a fair assessment? Then, because of specific things that the Prosecution has brought up in its case, I may be designating some more experts. If I do that, I will do that over the holidays as soon as I can find people who have expertise in various areas. But right now, we are just -- we need to also go over the testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know you might be waiting until after your submission, then you know what is left for you to defend. I think that is the normal pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is the other thing, your Honour. We do not know until the Trial Chamber rules on our submission what is left. So it would seem to be a waste of resources if we were to line up witnesses and have them standing out in the hallway having been flown in from every place and then have the Trial Chamber rule that as a matter of law we are dismissing that count on the indictment. So before we can really firm things up, we need to see how the Trial Chamber rules on our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So we start with a conservative fortnight period after the close of the case of the Prosecution, within which you will be able to submit your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is more than reasonable. We discussed this -- I want to say in October -- that I think everyone agreed, including the Trial Chamber, that two weeks for us to prepare it after the Prosecutor rests, two weeks for them to reply and a week for us to reply to their reply would be a reasonable time. I am just thinking off the top of my head right now, but there is enough time between now and January 12th that if we are fairly sure that the Prosecutor is going to rest that week, the other Trial Chambers could make plans to make use of the courtroom during that five week period. Also I think the Trial Chamber might want to also think about whether it would want to set aside a day or two days to argue that submission, for oral argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That depends on submissions of the answers themselves, so that we know what to do after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, where do you come in here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We have no particular opposition to the timetable proposed, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is the time scheduled that we are considering, the fortnight period for each one to submit and reply is adequate for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that is adequate for us, the time limits that were mentioned by Mr. Ackerman are suitable for the Prosecution, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will give also our own undertaking that as much as we can, every outstanding -- because there are a few outstanding rulings we must make sure to get to everyone before these things start. We will make sure that those things are cleared up and avoid any confusion while we go along, so we must make sure. So we too will be going for our Christmas vacation, those of us who come from very far away, so we hope to do that for the time being. So we thank you very much for now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just wonder whether or not Defence counsel can give us an idea of the order in which they proceed and if the Defence counsel, other than Mr. Ackerman, can give us a general idea of approximately how many witnesses they plan on calling, because it will also affect the Prosecution and its planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a good idea. These are very important things, so that we know exactly what the Prosecution faces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not hear Mr. Ackerman mentioning any numbers. I heard Mr. Moran mention some numbers, but I think that a long time ago, we discussed the matter, and I was joking at the time, but, of course, we will ask for a dismissal of the charges against our client, so that the Defence cannot at this stage give any rough estimate of the number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If we are expected to answer this question, like my learned colleague, Ms. Residovic, we also cannot know at this stage how many witnesses we will call, but they will certainly not be large numbers. Please do not hold me by what I say, but it will be ten to fifteen witnesses, and this number includes the expert witnesses that we intend to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, although Ms. McHenry was not interested in what I might have to say --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I apologise for getting the name wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Two little bearded guys from Texas tends to get mixed up at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could add something, I think I am much younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based on the assumption, and it is only an assumption and it probably will turn out to be untrue, but based on the assumption that we will be answering all the indictment as it currently exists, my estimate will be similar to that of Mr. Olujic, somewhere between ten and fifteen witnesses. In that group there will be two or three experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose it is fair not to be too much of a cock-eyed optimist. You cannot indicate the number of witnesses you want in case nothing happens to your optimism. Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Just raising the question that was raised by Madam Residovic, I just wish to say that in a recent matter which was before another Chamber, where Judge Cassese is the presiding judge, the Defence were ordered to produce not only their list of witnesses but witness statements prior to the commencement of the trial, which is an even earlier stage than suggested by Madam Residovic. In that case, there was an order made, so I do not see that the fact that she may make a submission of no case, if she is successful, true it is she will not call witnesses, but surely she is in a position to let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Could I just enquire from Mr. Niemann -- he is not listening. I would just like to enquire from Mr. Niemann which case that is so we can get a copy of the decision. Like a magpie, I gather little things like that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may be interested in that case. It is Dokmanovic. Not only was an order made to produce the Defence statements and the Defence list, the Prosecution statements and all exhibits were to be made available prior to the commencement of trial, and orders were entered to that effect. In addition to that, the Defence are required to indicate the grounds of their Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Most kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was also a request that we indicate an order, and it is my understanding that counsel have agreed that the presentation of the Defence will be in the order that they are named in the indictment. Before I sit down for the last time today, I want to wish everyone in this Trial Chamber, this Celebici family that we have been together with so long, very, very happy and healthy holidays, whatever that holiday may be for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it is a very good idea for Defence counsel to start preparing their list of witnesses so that they might not be caught unawares, and submit them, usually, in accordance with Rule 66 and Rule 67, if there is any reason why it is necessary to adhere to the Rules, because we do not want to be getting into the skirmish which we have been used to where there is obligation to do so because it makes the practice much easier for everyone, the statements which your witnesses are likely to cover, because the Prosecution will need them. We have taken it for granted that this is a normal thing. From what I have observed here, the practice has been going on, so that I do not expect it to be ignored now, that it has been going on for so long. I wish everyone a good Christmas, peaceful holiday and fully refreshed to start again on 12th January. As you said, as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, we will make sure that by the time you are due to start, you will have everything which we ought to do to enable you carry on. We will not fail in that regard, I assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you leave, I got the impression that the Trial Chamber expected us to deliver to the Prosecutor a witness list. As I recall on, I believe 21st February, you entered an order saying that there was no such obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Under Rule 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And 67. So, as I understand it, this point, unless there is a motion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are circumstances where you are obliged, it depends on the nature of your Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Short of an insanity defence or an alibi or something, the court is not posing any obligation. Thank you very much, your Honour, and have a good holiday. (5.15 pm)
